highlights: General MacArthur established GHQ SCAP in Tokyo on 2 October 1945 and activated nine Special Staff Sections to supervise non-military occupation policy, governing indirectly through the Japanese Government.
SCAP's 4 October 'Bill of Rights' directive repealed the Peace Preservation Law, abolished the thought-control police (4,800 officials dismissed), and freed 507 political prisoners.
Prime Minister Prince Higashikuni's Cabinet resigned en bloc on 5 October after the civil liberties directive and was replaced on 9 October by Baron Kijuro Shidehara's Cabinet.

The four major Zaibatsu combines, Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Yasuda and Sumitomo, agreed to voluntary dissolution plans transferring holding company securities to a liquidation commission; 29 wartime colonial banks were closed.
SCAP ordered the arrest of former Premier Hideki Tojo, his Pearl Harbor Cabinet and about 300 suspected war criminals.

Coal production fell from 3.4 million metric tons in June 1945 to under 600,000 tons in October after forced laborers were liberated, while typhoons worsened food shortages and the staple ration fell to 294 grams.

General MacArthur proclaimed U.S. Military Government in Korea on 7 September 1945, refusing recognition to domestic provisional regimes amid partition at the 38th parallel and 54 rival political parties.
Active Japanese merchant shipping shrank to 908,000 gross tons, mostly allocated to coastal coal and repatriation, while black-market prices reached up to 260 times official ceilings.

sections.summary: Title page, document documentation sheet, War Department transmittal memorandum and general table of contents for the first monthly summation.
sections.title: Front Matter

sections.summary: Executive overview of SCAP organization, early political and social reforms, economic demilitarization and stabilization in Japan, and U.S. Military Government civil administration in Korea.
sections.title: Part I: General

sections.summary: GHQ SCAP was established in Tokyo with nine Special Staff Sections, governing indirectly through the Japanese Government's Central Liaison Office; the section also outlines the Military Government framework in Korea.
sections.title: Section 1. Organization under SCAP

sections.summary: The 4 October 'Bill of Rights' directive toppled the Higashikuni Cabinet in favor of Shidehara's, 4,800 thought-police officials were dismissed, political prisoners freed, new parties emerged, and war crimes arrests began.
sections.title: Section 2. Political and Social Activities in Japan

sections.summary: War industries were demilitarized and Zaibatsu dissolution planned; trade unions were legalized, coal and food were scarce, trade and exchange were tightly controlled, and 29 wartime colonial banks were closed.
sections.title: Section 3. Economic Activities in Japan

sections.summary: U.S. Military Government in South Korea began operating under the 38th parallel division, replaced Japanese personnel, faced dozens of political factions and coal shortages, and moved to prevent winter typhus.
sections.title: Section 4. Civil Administration in Korea

sections.summary: Government administration, political reorganization, legal affairs, public safety and intelligence in Japan, including the Cabinet change, demobilization, release of political prisoners, and arrest orders for Tojo and 300 suspected war criminals.
sections.title: Part II: Political

sections.summary: Indirect administration worked through the Diet and Ministries; Higashikuni's Cabinet fell and Shidehara's formed, governors were shaken up, constitutional revision committees began, woman suffrage was proposed, and rival parties emerged.
sections.title: Section 1. Government and Civil Administration

sections.summary: Armed forces were fully demobilized, peace preservation laws abrogated, political prisoners released, 4,800 secret police purged, arrest orders issued for Tojo and 300 war criminals, and press censorship implemented.
sections.title: Section 2. Legal, Public Safety and Intelligence

sections.summary: Economic conditions in Japan: food and coal collapse, stagnant industry, crippled transport, controlled foreign trade, unemployment, black markets, and finance including closure of 29 colonial banks and Zaibatsu dissolution plans.
sections.title: Part III: Economic

sections.summary: September typhoon damage to rice worsened food deficits; fishing zones were authorized despite fuel and net shortages, urban charcoal ran short, and coal output collapsed after forced laborers were liberated.
sections.title: Section 1. Natural Resources

sections.summary: Industry stagnated: monthly truck production was authorized, shipyards repaired around the clock, iron and steel fell with coal shortages, wartime control associations were slated for dissolution, and cyclotron research was restricted.
sections.title: Section 2. Industry

sections.summary: Railroads proved relatively resilient despite overcrowding while motor vehicles deteriorated severely; active merchant shipping shrank to 908,000 gross tons, allocated mainly to coastal coal and repatriation.
sections.title: Section 3. Transportation

sections.summary: Imports were limited to vital necessities paid for by approved exports; export surpluses such as raw silk were identified, emergency coal went to Korea and Hong Kong, and wartime military trading companies were reviewed.
sections.title: Section 4. Imports and Exports

sections.summary: Labor was procured for Allied forces and unemployment projected above four million; prewar labor protections returned, independent unions re-formed under a unified federation, and Korean and Chinese coal miners struck violently.
sections.title: Section 5. Labor

sections.summary: War-damaged telephone and telegraph networks were rehabilitated for Allied use, international radio circuits censored, seized military vacuum tubes redistributed, equipment manufacturing recovered slowly, and electronics research restricted.
sections.title: Section 6. Communications

sections.summary: Commodity distribution broke down; the staple food ration fell to 294 grams, newsprint and textiles ran short, black-market prices reached 260 times official ceilings, and price control reform was pursued.
sections.title: Section 7. Rationing and Price Control

sections.summary: Fiscal distress persisted with the currency stabilized at 42 billion yen; 29 wartime colonial banks were liquidated, gold and silver impounded, war damage insurance left unsettled, and Zaibatsu dissolution begun.
sections.title: Section 8. Finance

sections.summary: Public health, welfare, medical supplies, education reform, religious freedom, cultural preservation and media liberalization in Japan, including relief for over 83,000 persons and the dissolution of the Domei news monopoly.
sections.title: Part IV: Social Services

sections.summary: Hospital facilities were damaged; relief reached over 83,000 persons, venereal disease directives issued, typhus prevention applied to repatriates, military medical stockpiles transferred, and relief supplies delivered to Hiroshima.
sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare

sections.summary: Education was demilitarized and teachers screened, the Religious Bodies Law abolished, State Shinto separation planned, the Domei news monopoly dissolved, and democratic radio, film and theatrical programs introduced.
sections.title: Section 2. Education, Religion and Media of Expression

sections.summary: U.S. Army Military Government in South Korea: political developments, economic conditions and social affairs, including the partition at the 38th parallel, rice market, typhus immunization and refugee relief.
sections.title: Part V: Korea

sections.summary: Direct U.S. Military Government was established under the 38th parallel partition; Japanese officials and police were purged, 54 parties rivaled one another, Syngman Rhee returned, and trusteeship drew wide hostility.
sections.title: Section 1. Political

sections.summary: A free rice market was established; fertilizer and fuel were severely short after supplies from North Korea were cut, emergency coal came from Japan, railroads and communications were reorganized, and finances tightly controlled.
sections.title: Section 2. Economic

sections.summary: Secondary schools reopened with Korean-language instruction, Military Government press and radio services expanded, the Bureau of Public Health was created, mass typhus immunization ran, and refugees were relieved at Fusan and Seoul.
sections.title: Section 3. Social

summary: Covering the foundational two months of the Allied occupation (September–October 1945), this initial summation records the establishment of General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (GHQ/SCAP) in Tokyo under General Douglas MacArthur and the simultaneous installation of U.S. Army Military Government in South Korea under the XXIV Corps. In Japan, SCAP instituted indirect governance through the Japanese cabinet and Diet while enforcing rapid demilitarization, dissolving the imperial military, and issuing the historic 4 October 'Bill of Rights' directive. That directive abolished thought-control police, repealed repressive statutes like the Peace Preservation Act, freed political prisoners, precipitated the collapse of the Higashikuni Cabinet, and initiated constitutional revision. The report portrays widespread economic paralysis across both territories: catastrophic coal deficits following the liberation of Korean and Chinese forced laborers, acute food shortages worsened by devastating September typhoons, uncontrolled black markets, and fiscal turmoil. In Korea, authorities confronted the crippling economic and political division along the 38th parallel, the rise of dozens of competing political factions, and popular resistance to allied trusteeship. For historians, the report provides invaluable baseline statistical surveys, structural blueprints of occupation administration, and candid accounts of early policy improvisation.
